content.text:
## Bottom line

**Negotiate. Don’t accept the current offer immediately, but don’t walk away yet.**

This is a **solid Google L6 offer in isolation**, but it is **not yet a compelling offer for a happy, passively recruited Meta IC6 earning approximately $526,000**. On a four-year basis, Google is offering only about a **5% premium** before refresh grants—and you would be accepting switching risk, a potentially less attractive team or performance trajectory, and a substantial compensation drop in years three and four.

My recommendation:

- **Opening request:** $260,000 base, $1.4 million equity, and a $200,000 sign-on.
- **Good landing zone:** $250,000–$255,000 base, $1.2 million–$1.3 million equity, and $100,000–$150,000 sign-on.
- **Likely decision threshold:** I would want approximately **$600,000–$625,000 annualized four-year compensation**, excluding refreshers, to leave a job you like.
- **If they remain near the present offer:** stay at Meta unless the Google role has unusually strong career or personal upside.

## What the offer is actually worth

Google’s cash compensation is:

- Base: $235,000
- Target bonus: $47,000
- Cash target: **$282,000**
- Equity annualized over four years: $270,000
- Four-year average target compensation: **$552,000**

Compared with Meta:

|  | Meta | Google |
|---|---:|---:|
| Base | $240,000 | $235,000 |
| Target/expected bonus | $36,000 | $47,000 |
| Annualized equity | $250,000 | $270,000 |
| Annualized total | **$526,000** | **$552,000** |

That is only **$26,000 more per year**, or about **5%**.

Over four years, assuming flat stock prices, target bonuses, no raises, no refreshers, and your current Meta compensation continuing:

- Google: **$2.208 million**
- Meta: **$2.104 million**
- Google advantage: **$104,000 over four years**

That is a small premium for leaving voluntarily. One weak bonus, weaker Google refreshes, a delayed promotion, or a less favorable stock performance could erase it.

Current self-reported market data puts US Google L6 PM median compensation around $514,000, with a 90th percentile around $671,000; a separate Bay Area cut currently places the L6 median around $551,000. Therefore, your offer is approximately a median-market package—not a premium package for recruiting a satisfied Meta IC6. ([levels.fyi](https://www.levels.fyi/companies/google/salaries/product-manager/locations/san-francisco-bay-area))

## The vesting schedule matters enormously

Before evaluating or accepting, get the precise vesting schedule in writing.

Google’s current new-hire grants are commonly reported as vesting:

- Year 1: 38%
- Year 2: 32%
- Year 3: 20%
- Year 4: 10%

Refresh grants are generally reported as vesting evenly over four years, but your individual award documents control. ([thesimplemoney.com](https://thesimplemoney.com/employers/google/gsu-grants-and-vesting-schedule))

If that schedule applies to your $1.08 million grant:

| Year | New-hire equity | Cash target | TC before refreshers |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | $410,400 | $282,000 | **$692,400** |
| 2 | $345,600 | $282,000 | **$627,600** |
| 3 | $216,000 | $282,000 | **$498,000** |
| 4 | $108,000 | $282,000 | **$390,000** |

This makes the offer look excellent in years one and two but creates a major **year-four cliff**.

Your four-year average is still $552,000; front-loading does not increase the grant’s total value. It simply makes the package depend heavily on future refresh awards to remain competitive.

## How to treat refresh grants

**Give refreshers little or no value in your acceptance calculation.**

Google does have an annual process that determines salary, bonus, and equity refresh amounts based on factors such as role, location, performance and managerial discretion. That confirms refreshes are part of the compensation system, but it does not guarantee that you will receive a particular amount. ([services.google.com](https://services.google.com/fh/files/blogs/pay_equity_info_sheet.pdf))

The recruiter was appropriately explicit about that.

A useful way to look at it:

- Your Google cash target is $282,000.
- To maintain your present $526,000 Meta run rate, you need **$244,000 per year of vested Google stock**.
- By year four, only $108,000 of the initial grant is scheduled to vest under the 38/32/20/10 schedule.
- Therefore, you would need roughly **$136,000 of additional year-four vesting** from stacked refreshes merely to remain at your current Meta run rate—before accounting for raises or future Meta refreshers.

Refreshes may very well solve this, but that is an employment outcome, not part of the guaranteed offer.

## What to negotiate

### 1. Base: ask for $260,000

Your offered base is:

- $5,000 below your Meta base
- Well below the $271,000 top of the posted range
- Slightly below the approximately $240,000 recent US median reported for Google L6 PMs ([aakashg.com](https://www.aakashg.com/google-pm-job-offer/))

Ask for **$260,000**. A realistic landing point is probably **$250,000–$255,000**.

Base is particularly valuable because it:

- Recurs every year
- Raises your 20% bonus target
- Is not dependent on Alphabet’s stock price
- May influence future raises and internal compensation positioning

At $250,000, your bonus target becomes $50,000, giving you $300,000 of target cash.

### 2. Equity: ask for $1.4 million

The existing $1.08 million grant annualizes to $270,000. That makes the overall package only modestly better than Meta.

Ask for **$1.4 million**, expecting that they may land between **$1.2 million and $1.3 million**.

Examples:

| Base | Bonus | Equity grant | Four-year annualized TC |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Current offer: $235K | $47K | $1.08M | **$552K** |
| $250K | $50K | $1.20M | **$600K** |
| $250K | $50K | $1.30M | **$625K** |
| Opening ask: $260K | $52K | $1.40M | **$662K** |

A $600,000–$625,000 package represents approximately a **14%–19% premium** over your Meta run rate. That is much more appropriate for a voluntary switch from a position you like.

### 3. Sign-on: ask for $200,000

You have approximately $200,000 of Meta shares vesting over the next 12 months. Ask for a **$200,000 make-whole sign-on bonus**.

You may not get all of it. A good result would be:

- $100,000–$150,000 cash, or
- Additional equity of equivalent value, or
- A combination of cash and equity.

Cash is preferable if leaving Meta causes a meaningful gap between your final Meta vest and first Google vest.

Be sure to ask:

- Whether the sign-on is paid immediately or in installments
- Whether it has a one- or two-year repayment obligation
- Whether repayment is prorated
- What happens in an involuntary termination

## Suggested negotiation language

You can say:

> I’m genuinely excited about the role and team. At the same time, I wasn’t planning to leave Meta, and I’m currently at approximately $526,000 in annual compensation, with about $200,000 of equity scheduled to vest over the next 12 months.
>
> The current offer annualizes to approximately $552,000 over four years, so the premium over staying is relatively modest, particularly given the back-end decline in the new-hire equity schedule and the fact that future refresh grants aren’t guaranteed.
>
> For this move to make sense, I’d be looking for a package closer to $260,000 base, $1.4 million in new-hire equity, and a $200,000 sign-on bonus to address the equity I would be leaving behind. I’m flexible regarding the mix, and my priority is getting the four-year guaranteed value to a level that appropriately reflects the move from a role where I’m performing well and happy.

Then stop talking and let the recruiter respond.

If they say one component is constrained:

> I understand. If base or cash is constrained, I’d be open to solving more of the gap through the equity grant. My target is approximately $625,000 or more in annualized four-year compensation, plus some make-whole treatment for the near-term Meta vesting.

Only state that number if it is genuinely sufficient for you to accept.

## Information to obtain before accepting

Ask the recruiter to confirm in writing:

1. **Exact new-hire vesting percentages** and vesting dates.
2. **First vest date**, especially relative to your proposed start date.
3. Whether your first annual bonus will be **prorated**.
4. When you first become eligible for an equity refresh.
5. Whether refresh awards vest evenly or on another schedule.
6. Whether starting after a particular date affects refresh or bonus eligibility.
7. The grant-date mechanics used to determine your GSU share count.
8. Sign-on repayment terms if one is added.
9. Whether any portion of the offer expires or requires compensation committee approval.

Start-date timing could be worth tens of thousands of dollars if it lets you collect an imminent Meta vest without sacrificing Google bonus or refresh eligibility.

## Accept, negotiate, or walk?

### Accept as-is only if:

- The Google role is substantially better for your long-term trajectory;
- You strongly prefer the team, manager or product;
- You want diversification away from Meta;
- Or the first two years’ front-loaded compensation has special value to you.

### Negotiate if:

- You are interested but primarily motivated by compensation;
- You need a meaningful premium to leave;
- You would accept around $600,000–$625,000 annualized plus some make-whole compensation.

**This is my recommended path.**

### Walk away if:

- They make no meaningful improvement;
- The vesting or start-date mechanics are worse than expected;
- The team or manager is merely comparable rather than clearly better;
- Or you would feel underpaid once compensation falls below Meta levels in years three and four.

The clean characterization is:

> **It’s a good market offer, but not yet a good switching offer for you.**

Because you are happy at Meta and Google initiated the process, your reservation price should be high. I would negotiate aggressively, aim to land around **$250,000–$255,000 base, $1.2 million–$1.3 million equity and $100,000–$150,000 sign-on**, and be comfortable staying at Meta if Google cannot get reasonably close.

content.text:
## My lean: **take it**, assuming you like the manager, team, and scope

The revised offer clears the compensation bar. It is no longer merely a market-rate offer—it provides a meaningful premium over your current Meta compensation **without assigning any value to future Google refresh grants**.

### Four-year comparison

Assuming target bonuses, constant stock prices, and no future refreshes at either company:

|  | Meta | Google |
|---|---:|---:|
| Base | $240K | $240K |
| Bonus | ~$36K | $48K target |
| Annualized equity | ~$250K | $320K |
| Annualized total | **$526K** | **$608K** |
| Four-year total | **$2.104M** | **$2.432M** |

Google is now ahead by:

- **$82,000 per year**
- **$328,000 over four years**
- Approximately **15.6%**

That is within the range I would consider sufficient for a voluntary move from a job you like. The revised offer is also above the current self-reported US median of about $576,000 for Google L6 PMs. ([levels.fyi](https://www.levels.fyi/companies/google/salaries/product-manager/locations/united-states))

## The likely annual breakdown

You must confirm your exact schedule, but Google new-hire grants are commonly reported as vesting **38% / 32% / 20% / 10%**. Alphabet officially confirms that employee RSUs generally vest over four years, while the individual award controls. ([thesimplemoney.com](https://thesimplemoney.com/employers/google/gsu-grants-and-vesting-schedule))

Under 38/32/20/10:

| Year | Google equity | Base + target bonus | Google TC |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | $486.4K | $288K | **$774.4K** |
| 2 | $409.6K | $288K | **$697.6K** |
| 3 | $256K | $288K | **$544K** |
| 4 | $128K | $288K | **$416K** |
| Average | $320K | $288K | **$608K** |

Compared with a flat $526,000 Meta run rate, the differences are approximately:

- Year 1: **+$248K**
- Year 2: **+$172K**
- Year 3: **+$18K**
- Year 4: **−$110K**

So this is effectively a highly front-loaded package. You are being paid very well to switch, but you will need refresh grants to prevent a large year-four decline.

Google does run an annual process that determines equity refresh amounts based on factors including role, location, performance, and managerial discretion, but that does not guarantee any specific refresh. ([services.google.com](https://services.google.com/fh/files/blogs/pay_equity_info_sheet.pdf))

## The missing sign-on is no longer a major problem

Google effectively responded to your $200,000 forfeiture by adding **$200,000 to the equity grant**.

That is not identical to a $200,000 cash sign-on:

- Only $76,000 of the incremental $200,000 would vest in year one under a 38% schedule.
- You bear Alphabet stock-price and continued-employment risk.
- The remainder is spread across subsequent years.

Nevertheless, your **total first-year Google equity would be approximately $486,400**, versus the roughly $200,000 you would receive from Meta over the next 12 months. Your first-year Google compensation would therefore be about **$774,400**, versus approximately **$476,000 at Meta** if the $200,000 figure represents your actual next-12-month Meta vesting.

In other words, you are not economically behind in year one merely because there is no sign-on.

## Reasons I would still stay at Meta

I would decline Google despite the compensation if any of the following apply:

1. **You have a credible near-term Meta promotion path.**  
   A realistic IC7 promotion within roughly 12–18 months could change the comparison substantially.

2. **Meta is likely to give you an unusually large refresh soon.**  
   Compare the Google offer against your actual forward Meta vesting schedule and likely upcoming refresh—not just your trailing compensation.

3. **The Google role has less scope or a questionable manager.**  
   A weak first assignment could hurt performance, refreshes, and future promotion prospects. At this level, manager and organizational placement can be worth more than an extra $82,000 annually.

4. **You strongly prefer Meta and require a 20%–25% switching premium.**  
   A 20% premium over $526,000 would be about $631,000. Google is at $608,000, so it is strong but not overwhelming.

5. **You expect to leave Google quickly.**  
   Although the package is front-loaded, unvested equity disappears when you leave. Confirm the first vest timing and whether the grant vests monthly, quarterly, or on another schedule.

## What to confirm before signing

Since they have called this their best offer, I would stop negotiating compensation. Get these details in writing:

1. Exact vesting percentages—do not assume 38/32/20/10.
2. Vesting frequency and first vest date.
3. Grant date and the method used to calculate the number of shares.
4. Whether your first bonus is prorated.
5. When you first become eligible for a refresh.
6. Whether your start date affects bonus or refresh eligibility.
7. Whether you can time your start date immediately after an upcoming Meta vest.

The final item may be your remaining opportunity to add value. You can say:

> I understand the compensation is final, and I appreciate the movement on equity. Before signing, I’d like to coordinate the start date around my existing vesting schedule. Would a start date of [date immediately after the next Meta vest] work for the team?

That is a logistics request, not another compensation negotiation.

## Recommendation

**I would accept if:**

- The Google role and manager are at least reasonably attractive;
- You do not expect an imminent Meta promotion or exceptional refresh;
- You are comfortable treating years one and two as unusually high-compensation years rather than increasing your permanent spending; and
- The written vesting schedule is what you expect.

I would sell enough vested Google shares to diversify and save a significant portion of the first two years’ premium, because the year-four cliff is real.

**Verdict: accept, with one final vesting-schedule and start-date check.** The revised offer pays approximately a 16% four-year premium before refreshes and adequately addresses the economic cost of leaving Meta, even though it does so through equity rather than a sign-on bonus.
